title: Car jerks when accelerating
h1: Why does my car jerk when I accelerate?
metaDesc: Car jerks or bucks when you press the gas? Find out if it's a misfire, fuel, the transmission or a worn mount, how urgent it is, and what to tell your mechanic.
synonyms: car jerking when I press the gas
car jerks when i give it gas
car jerks and check engine light flashing
intro: A jerk or buck when you press the gas usually comes from the engine stumbling, the transmission shifting badly, or worn parts letting the engine rock. When it happens and what the dash shows are the best clues. Answer a few questions to see the likely causes and how soon to deal with it.
safety: If the check engine light is flashing, or the car is shaking, pull over and stop driving it.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, pull over, turn the engine off and get away from the car.
If the car suddenly loses power in traffic, turn on your hazards and get to the shoulder.

q_light.q: Is the check engine light on right now?
q_light.help: The check engine light is the engine-shaped symbol, usually yellow or orange. A flashing light is more serious than a steady one.

opts.a: As the automatic transmission changes gears: a hard bump or slam
Cruising gently around 30 to 50 mph, like driving over rumble strips
When I press the gas harder, pull away or climb a hill: the engine stumbles or bucks
Only when I first press the gas or lift off: a single clunk or jolt
It's a manual, and it bucks or shudders as I let the clutch out

q_engine.help: These clues separate an ignition problem from a fuel or air problem.

opts.a: It's worse on damp or rainy days, or the engine also shakes when idling
It sputters and loses power like it's starving, especially uphill or at higher speeds
It hesitates and then surges, or the idle is uneven and I hear a hiss
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be misfiring badly enough to cause damage
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Have the car towed or call a mobile mechanic instead of continuing on.
if: If the light stops flashing after a restart, don't trust it. The fault is still there, so get it checked before using the car.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, step away from the car and call for help.
If the temperature gauge is high or the oil pressure light is on, don't restart the engine.
result.why: A flashing check engine light usually means the engine computer has detected misfires severe enough to damage the catalytic converter. Unburned fuel goes into the exhaust and can overheat it. The jerking you feel is likely cylinders cutting in and out.

causes.name: Failed ignition coil or spark plug
causes.clues: The jerk is strongest under load, and the engine also shakes at idle.

causes.name: Fuel injector stuck or not working
causes.clues: The misfire stays on the same cylinder even after the coil is swapped.

causes.name: Internal engine problem, such as low compression
causes.clues: Ticking or knocking, oil or coolant loss, or a misfire that doesn't move when the coil and plug are swapped between cylinders.
causes.against: Much less common than coil or spark plug problems.

you: Note what you were doing when the light started flashing.
Note any other warning lights on the dash.
shop: Code scan and misfire counts by cylinder
Ignition coil and spark plug inspection

result.title: An engine fault is stored. The code will narrow it down
result.now: Have the trouble codes read within the next few days. Many auto parts stores do it free. Drive gently until then and avoid hard acceleration.
if: If the light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the code points to the transmission, keep trips short and get it checked as soon as you can.
If the car loses power, starts shaking harder, or you smell fuel, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: A steady check engine light means the computer has found a fault, but not one it treats as immediately damaging. Jerking with a steady light is often an early misfire, a fuel delivery problem or a sensor giving bad readings. The stored code tells the shop where to start.

causes.name: Early misfire from a worn spark plug or ignition coil
causes.clues: The jerk is worse under load or uphill, and the engine may shake at idle.

causes.name: Faulty sensor, such as the airflow or throttle sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation followed by a surge, or worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering at higher speeds or on hills.

you: Get the codes read and write down the full letters and numbers.
Note when the jerk happens: speed, how hard you press the gas, and whether the engine is cold or warm.

result.title: Possibly a misfire from a worn spark plug or ignition coil
result.now: Book a check within the next few days, and avoid hard acceleration until then.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the spark plugs are past the replacement interval in your owner's manual, tell the shop.
If the car loses power in traffic or you smell fuel, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: When a spark plug or coil is weak, a cylinder can fail to fire just when the engine is working hardest. You feel that as a jerk or buck. Moisture makes weak ignition parts worse, which is why it can be worse on damp days. A shop will usually find which cylinder is misfiring and swap parts between cylinders to test before replacing anything.

causes.name: Worn spark plugs
causes.clues: High mileage, or plugs past their replacement interval.
causes.against: Less likely if the plugs were replaced recently.

causes.name: Failing ignition coil or plug wire
causes.clues: Worse in damp weather, or a check engine light that comes and goes.

causes.name: Clogged or failing fuel injector
causes.clues: A misfire on one cylinder that doesn't move when the coil is swapped.

you: Check your service records for the last spark plug change.
Have the codes read if the check engine light has come on, even briefly.

result.title: The engine may not be getting enough fuel under load
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. Until then, keep the tank above a quarter full and avoid hard acceleration and long climbs.
if: If it starts stalling or losing power in traffic, stop driving it and have it towed.
If it began right after a fill-up, tell the shop. Bad or watery fuel can cause this.
If you smell raw fuel, stop driving it and have it towed. A fuel leak is a fire risk.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: When you accelerate hard, the engine needs much more fuel. A weak fuel pump, a clogged filter or dirty injectors may keep up at idle but fall short when you ask for power, so the engine sputters and jerks. A shop will usually test fuel pressure and volume before replacing a pump.

causes.name: Weak fuel pump
causes.clues: Worse uphill, at higher speeds or when the tank is low.

causes.name: Clogged fuel filter
causes.clues: A slow loss of power over months, on cars that have a replaceable filter.

causes.name: Dirty or failing fuel injectors
causes.clues: A rough idle and worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Contaminated fuel
causes.clues: It started suddenly right after a fill-up.

you: Notice whether it's worse when the tank is low.
Think back to whether it started right after a fill-up.
shop: Fuel pressure and volume test under load

result.title: An air leak or a dirty airflow sensor may be throwing off the fuel mix
result.now: Book a check when convenient. A shop can find most air leaks quickly with a smoke test.
if: If the check engine light comes on or the hesitation gets worse, get it checked within a few days.
If the engine starts stalling at stops, have it looked at before relying on the car.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
result.why: The engine computer measures the air coming in to decide how much fuel to add. A cracked vacuum hose lets in air it didn't measure, and a dirty airflow sensor misreads it. Either way the mix comes out wrong, so the car hesitates and then surges.

causes.name: Vacuum leak from a cracked hose or intake gasket
causes.clues: A hissing sound, or a high or uneven idle.

causes.name: Dirty or faulty mass airflow sensor
causes.clues: Hesitation then surge, and worse fuel economy.

causes.name: Dirty throttle body
causes.clues: A rough idle, or the car feels sticky right off the pedal.

you: With the engine idling and the car in Park, listen from the front of the car for a hiss.
With the engine off, look for cracked or loose rubber hoses on top of the engine.
Check that the air filter isn't badly clogged.
shop: Code scan and live airflow data

result.title: The automatic transmission may be shifting harshly
result.now: Book a transmission check within the next few days. Until then, accelerate gently and avoid towing or heavy loads.
if: If the engine revs but the car doesn't speed up, or a transmission warning light comes on, stop driving and have it towed.
If you see red or pink fluid where you park, tell the shop. Low fluid causes harsh shifts.
If you smell burning from under the car, stop driving and have it checked.
result.why: A jolt right as the gears change usually means the transmission isn't controlling the shift smoothly. Low or worn-out fluid, a shift control problem or worn internal parts can all cause it. Catching it early often keeps the repair smaller, and a shop will usually check fluid, codes and software before suggesting major work.

causes.name: Low or worn-out transmission fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or fluid that's dark and smells burnt.

causes.name: Shift solenoid or transmission control fault
causes.clues: A transmission warning light, or shifts that are smooth sometimes and harsh other times.

causes.name: Worn internal clutches
causes.clues: High mileage, slipping, or harsh shifts that keep getting worse.

you: If your car has a transmission dipstick, check the level and color the way your owner's manual describes. Many are checked with the engine warm and running.
Look for red or pink spots where you park.
shop: Road test with live transmission data

result.title: This may be torque converter shudder
result.now: Book a transmission check when convenient. Tell the shop it feels like rumble strips at steady, light cruising.
if: If it gets worse quickly, or you notice slipping or a transmission warning light, get it checked within a few days.
If you see red or pink fluid under the car, get it checked sooner.
If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving. That points to an engine misfire.
result.why: The torque converter connects the engine to an automatic transmission. At steady, light cruising it locks up to save fuel, and if that lockup clutch grabs unevenly, the car shudders as if crossing rumble strips. Worn fluid is a common cause, and it tends to get worse over time. A shop will usually check the fluid and any updates or service bulletins before replacing the converter.

causes.name: Worn or contaminated transmission fluid
causes.clues: The fluid hasn't been changed in a long time, or it looks dark.

causes.name: Worn torque converter lockup clutch
causes.clues: The shudder stops when you press harder or lift off the gas.

causes.name: Engine misfire under light load
causes.clues: A check engine light, or a shake at idle.
causes.against: A misfire usually feels worse when you press harder, not lighter.

you: Note the speed range where it happens.
Notice whether a little more or a little less gas makes it stop.
shop: Road test watching torque converter lockup data

result.title: Possibly worn engine mounts or play in the drive axles
result.now: Book a check when convenient, and ask the shop to inspect the engine and transmission mounts and the drive axles.
if: If you hear a loud bang, or the clunk is getting worse quickly, get it checked within a few days.
If you also hear clicking when turning sharply, a worn axle joint is a possibility. Get it checked soon.
result.why: Mounts are rubber blocks that hold the engine and transmission in place. When they wear out, the engine rocks when you get on or off the gas, and you feel it as a clunk or jolt. Worn axle joints can feel very similar.

causes.name: Worn or broken engine or transmission mount
causes.clues: A clunk when shifting into Drive or Reverse, or more vibration at idle.

causes.name: Worn CV joint or U-joint
causes.clues: Clicking when turning, or a clunk that seems to come from under the car rather than the engine bay.

causes.name: Loose exhaust hanger or heat shield
causes.clues: A thump or rattle along with the clunk.

you: Notice whether the clunk also happens when shifting into Drive or Reverse.
Listen for clicking while making slow, tight turns in an empty parking lot.
shop: Drive axle, CV joint and U-joint check

result.title: The clutch may be grabbing unevenly (clutch chatter)
result.now: Book a check when convenient. Until then, let the clutch out slowly and smoothly.
if: If the engine revs but the car doesn't speed up in higher gears, the clutch is slipping. Get it checked within a few days.
If you smell burning after pulling away, avoid slipping the clutch and get it checked soon.
If you see smoke from under the car, stop and have it towed.
result.why: When the clutch grabs unevenly as you let it out, the car shudders or bucks. Oil on the clutch, worn clutch parts or weak engine mounts are the usual reasons.

causes.name: Contaminated or worn clutch disc
causes.clues: Chatter that's worse when hot, or a burning smell.

causes.name: Worn engine or transmission mounts
causes.clues: A clunk along with the chatter.

causes.name: Worn or uneven flywheel
causes.clues: Chatter plus vibration you can feel through the pedal.

you: Notice whether it's worse when the car is fully warmed up.
Look for oil drips between the engine and the transmission.
shop: Check for an oil leak onto the clutch

result.title: Jerking needs a code scan and a short road test to pin down
result.now: Have the codes read and book a check. Tell the shop when the jerk happens: speed, how hard you press the gas, and whether the engine is cold or warm.
if: If the check engine light starts flashing, pull over and stop driving.
If the jerking gets worse or the car starts losing power, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you smell fuel or see smoke, pull over, turn off the engine and get away from the car.
result.why: Jerking can come from the engine, the transmission or worn mounts, and they can feel alike from the driver's seat. A code scan plus a short road test usually separates them quickly.

causes.name: Ignition misfire
causes.clues: Worse under load or uphill.

causes.name: Fuel delivery problem
causes.clues: Sputtering at higher speeds.

causes.name: Transmission shift problem
causes.clues: It happens exactly as the gears change.

you: Keep notes on when it happens.
Have the codes read even with no light on. Some faults are stored before the light comes on.
